In Ambonese Malay, the alignment of sentence-final pitch peaks fails to support the existence of either word stress or phrase-final pitch accents. Also, the shape of its pitch peaks fails to vary systematically with the information status of the phrase-final word. The two intonation melodies of the language include phrase-final boundary-tone complexes which do not associate with any syllables. The declarative rise-fall would appear to be timed so as to occur within the last word of the sentence. new_statements.quote: In a description of Ambonese Malay, van Minde (1997) assumed irregular word stress. No indications are given about the (default) location of word stress and, crucially, no report on the existence of schwa is provided (Paauw 2009). The main reason for irregularity is the phonemic nature of stress; hence the minimal pair /ˈba.rat/ ‘west’ and /ba.ˈrat/ ‘heavy’. However, a re-evaluation and acoustic measurements were carried out on read speech samples from four speakers (Maskikit-Essed & Gussenhoven 2016). The samples were comparable to the ones in van Minde (1997) and led to the conclusion that word stress does not exist in Ambonese Malay.

new_statements.relation_note: Same coding as the catalog (no-word-stress, Maskikit-Essed & Gussenhoven 2016). Adds the specific reason the earlier lexical-stress claim was dropped (six-vowel reanalysis; no duration/F0/spectral-tilt correlates) and records van Minde's claim as irregular/phonemic with no default position.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Survey classification: Ambonese Malay has no word stress. Van Minde 1997 had claimed phonemic, irregularly placed stress with no default position; the acoustic study of Maskikit-Essed & Gussenhoven 2016 (four speakers, read speech) found no reliable stress correlates in duration, F0 peak alignment or spectral tilt, reanalysed the 'unstressed' /a/ of the minimal pairs as a separate phoneme (a-caduc), and found no pitch accents either. p. 129 adds: 'Ambonese Malay was shown to lack word stress (Maskikit-Essed & Gussenhoven 2016), counter to the P;U (LEX) claim in van Minde (1997). A small effect of spectral tilt could be found, but no systematic acoustic differences due to stress in duration or F0.'
new_statements.exceptions: Kaland (p. 97, sec. 4.1.2) cautions that the 2016 no-stress analysis rests on a small number of speakers and that van Minde's evidence was impressionistic minimal pairs; he calls for further empirical work but adopts the no-stress reading throughout.
new_statements.identity_note: van Minde 1997 describes 'Malayu Ambong', the Malay of Ambon town and island; Maskikit-Essed & Gussenhoven 2016 worked from four Ambonese Malay speakers reading material comparable to van Minde's (per Kaland 2025 p. 15). Paauw 2008's stress sentence is about reconstructed Vehicular Malay / North Moluccan Malay, not Ambon specifically. Erniati 2019 (not opened) is titled as the Ambon dialect of Malay.

new_statements.rule_in_words: As paraphrased from van Minde 1997: stress is phonemic and its position in the word cannot be predicted; minimal pairs differ only in stress (penultimate vs final). Van Minde (p. 22) also marks stress on both halves of lexically reduplicated morphemes (/’eleK’eleK/, /t’omit’omi/) but not on duplicated monosyllables (/pomp’om/).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Both roots of a lexically reduplicated morpheme carry a marked stress (p. 22); nothing labelled 'secondary'.
new_statements.exceptions: Duplicated monosyllables carry a single stress (p. 22).

readall_conflicts: The only substantive disagreement is the known one: van Minde 1997 (pp. 21-23, seen here only through Wikipedia's page-cited paraphrase and Kaland 2025's summary) describes phonemic, unpredictably placed word stress with minimal pairs (/'barat/ 'west' vs /ba'rat/ 'heavy', /p'araN/ 'machete' vs /par'aN/ 'war'), and Paauw 2008 (p. 99) repeats the pre-instrumental view for the eastern varieties generally (penult, final if the penult had schwa, phonemic after schwa loss). Maskikit-Essed & Gussenhoven 2016 (catalog deciding source; abstract plus the open erratum) found no acoustic correlates of stress or pitch accent in four speakers and reanalysed the minimal pairs as a segmental /a/ vs weak /ă/ contrast; Kaland 2025 (pp. 15, 18, 97, 129-131) adopts that no-stress reading while noting the small speaker sample. the listed work (van Minde) could not be opened, so its stress statement remains verified only second-hand.

sources.quote: No independent stress analysis for Ambon Malay: speaks of /i/~/e/, /u/~/o/ alternation 'in final unstressed syllables of polysyllabic morphemes' following van Minde (1997: 25-29); the explicit 'loss of the schwa has led to the development of phonemic stress ... ba'rat heavy / 'barat west' statement (p. 99) is made for North Moluccan/Vehicular Malay, with Ambon said to have undergone 'similar' processes. Impressionistic, pre-2016; aligns with the van Minde srule, not with the deciding instrumental result.
